name: Evaluating a Pitch Deck
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Reading Between the Slides: A Field Guide to the Quantum Pitch Deck
lesson.summary: A pitch deck is a curated persuasion document, and evaluating one well means running the red flags checklist against its claims, watching your own biases compound in real time as the narrative lands, and pricing the ask with the same probability times impact math from risk assessment.
lesson.body:
A pitch deck is not a technical paper and was never meant to be one. It is a persuasion document, built by people who are, reasonably, trying to raise money, and every choice in it, what gets a slide, what gets a footnote, what gets left out entirely, is made with that goal in mind. That does not make a pitch deck dishonest by default. It does mean a deck is exactly the kind of document the last several chapters of this course prepared you to read closely rather than passively, because it is where a hyped technical claim, a set of cognitive biases, and a real financial ask all show up on the same page at once.

Picture a specific one. A company called Coherentix is raising a Series B, and the deck runs in a familiar order: the problem, the technology, traction, the team, a roadmap, and the ask. The technology slide states that Coherentix's approach delivers a "revolutionary 50x speedup" on a class of optimization problems, illustrated with a single bar chart and no named baseline. That is worth flagging on sight, a specific number dressed up next to a vague superlative, compared against an unnamed alternative, close to the weak baseline comparison pattern from red flags in tech claims, just with a number attached instead of an adjective alone. The traction slide shows glowing results from three enterprise pilots, all under NDA, none independently reproducible outside the company's own account of them. The roadmap slide is where the real tell shows up: eighteen months earlier, Coherentix's public materials promised a fault-tolerant quantum processor, and this year's deck has quietly narrowed that promise to a "quantum-inspired classical optimization engine," presented with exactly the same confident tone as if the original goal had been hit. Nobody on the roadmap slide acknowledges that the target moved. That is redefining success, and the deck's silence about why the goal changed is the actual signal, not the change itself.

None of that happens in a vacuum, and the investor sitting in the room is not a neutral instrument either. The moment the deck states its valuation, that number becomes an anchor for every negotiation that follows, no matter how it was derived. Learning that two respected funds are already committed to the round activates something close to bandwagon reasoning and a specific flavor of FOMO, the fear of being the investor who passed on the deal everyone else took. And once even a small amount of enthusiasm has taken hold, the customer testimonials on the traction slide get read charitably, three data points doing the work of thirty, because confirmation bias is already shaping which details register as important. This is the bias compounding loop from earlier in the course, showing up in real time, inside a single hour long meeting, not over years.

Running the risk assessment framework on the ask itself is what keeps the meeting from being decided by momentum alone. The two variables have to be estimated separately. Probability: Coherentix's actual advantage claim depends on an algorithmic breakthrough for that problem class, which earlier chapters placed on the deep uncertainty end of the seven required breakthroughs, not the engineering end, meaning more money and more time are not guaranteed to produce it on any particular schedule. Impact: the ask is a large check, meaningful dilution, and a multi year commitment of attention as much as capital. A deck that inspires confidence is not evidence of a high probability, and a large opportunity is not evidence that impact should be ignored. The two numbers get estimated on their own terms and then multiplied, not blended into a single feeling in the room.

The practical habit worth taking from this chapter is reading any pitch deck at least three separate times with three separate questions in mind: once for content, checking each specific claim against the red flags checklist, once for yourself, naming which biases the pitch is activating in you personally as it plays out, and once for stakes, running probability against impact on the actual ask rather than the story around it. None of this requires assuming Coherentix is lying. It requires refusing to let a well built narrative substitute for that separate accounting. The same three passes scale up directly to the boardroom, where the ask gets larger, the stakes get higher, and a different set of tools, covered later in this course, comes into play alongside this one.
